beats.headline: Your background tasks are leaking memory.
beats.subline: Standard ExecutorService creates orphan threads that run forever even after the parent fails.
beats.narration: If your travel booking service fails, does it actually stop the background flight and hotel calls? With standard ExecutorService, those tasks become orphans, wasting resources and potentially booking ghost trips.

beats.title: Unstructured vs Structured

top.label: ExecutorService
top.code:
Future<Flight> f = exec.submit(task);
// If this fails, 'task' keeps running!

beats.narration: In unstructured code, the parent thread doesn't own the subtask lifecycle. Structured concurrency forces subtasks to finish before the block exits, ensuring no background work escapes your control.

beats.title: ShutdownOnFailure Policy

steps.explanation: The try-with-resources block ensures that if any task fails, the scope cleans up everything.
Spawns a virtual thread. If one fails, the other is automatically interrupted.

beats.narration: ShutdownOnFailure is the gold standard for atomic operations. If reserveHotel fails, the scope immediately interrupts the flight task, preventing any partial state corruption.

beats.title: Cancellation Cascade
beats.narration: When a subtask fails, the scope triggers a cancellation cascade. It interrupts all siblings, waits for them to terminate, and only then throws the exception to the parent.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Racing providers with ShutdownOnSuccess →
beats.narration: That's the foundation of structured concurrency. In Part 2, we explore how to race multiple redundant service providers and pick the fastest result.

beats.headline: Stop waiting for the slowest provider.
beats.subline: ShutdownOnSuccess automatically kills redundant calls the moment you get a winner.
beats.narration: Why wait for three pricing feeds when you only need one? ShutdownOnSuccess lets you race providers, taking the first valid result and killing the losers instantly.

beats.title: Racing Redundant Feeds

steps.explanation: As soon as one task succeeds, the scope cancels the other two.
Returns the winner. If all fail, it throws an ExecutionException.

beats.narration: Unlike CompletableFuture, this handles early failures gracefully. If Bloomberg fails but Reuters succeeds, you get the Reuters rate. The scope only fails if every single provider throws an error.

beats.title: Enforcing Hard Deadlines

steps.explanation: Throws TimeoutException if the scope doesn't finish by the deadline.
On timeout, the scope shuts down and interrupts all pending tasks.

beats.narration: Never let a request hang forever. joinUntil sets a hard limit. If the deadline passes, the scope automatically cancels all pending work, keeping your system responsive.

beats.title: Java 25 API Evolution
beats.caption: The API is moving to static factories
beats.narration: Java 25 simplifies the API. Instead of constructors, you use static factories. The underlying mechanics of lexical containment and sibling cancellation remain identical.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): Why ScopedValue kills ThreadLocal →
beats.narration: You now have total control over subtask lifecycles. In Part 3, we replace the leaky ThreadLocal with ScopedValue to pass context safely across virtual threads.

beats.headline: ThreadLocal is a memory leak waiting to happen.
beats.subline: ScopedValue provides immutable, bounded context sharing that is perfect for virtual threads.
beats.narration: ThreadLocal is a trap. It's mutable, leaks memory in thread pools, and is expensive to copy. ScopedValue is the modern, immutable replacement for passing context like trace IDs.

beats.title: ThreadLocal vs ScopedValue
beats.narration: ScopedValue is immutable. Once bound, it stays that way for the duration of the block. No more manual removal, no more cross-request data leaks.

beats.title: Binding Context

steps.explanation: Define your context key as a constant.
Binds the value only for the duration of the lambda.

beats.narration: The binding is strictly scoped to the run block. Once the lambda finishes, the value is unbound. It's impossible to leak this context into other threads.

beats.title: Zero-Copy Inheritance
beats.narration: When you fork a subtask inside a StructuredTaskScope, it automatically sees the parent's ScopedValue. It's a direct reference, not a copy, making it incredibly fast.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In

beats.narration: You've mastered context sharing. In Part 4, we look at how the JVM makes these task hierarchies visible in thread dumps for production debugging.

beats.headline: Stop debugging flat thread lists.
beats.subline: Structured concurrency groups threads by hierarchy, making production debugging actually readable.
beats.narration: Ever looked at a thread dump and seen thousands of unrelated threads? Structured concurrency fixes this. The JVM now groups virtual threads by their scope hierarchy.

beats.title: Hierarchical Thread Dumps
beats.caption: jcmd shows the task tree
beats.narration: When you dump threads, you see the tree. You can instantly identify which parent request spawned a stuck subtask, drastically reducing your mean time to resolution.

beats.title: The Golden Rule of Interruption
beats.narration: Cancellation is cooperative. If you swallow an InterruptedException, the scope can't kill your task. Always restore the flag to allow the scope to terminate properly.

beats.title: The Unified Model
beats.narration: Combine these two and you get a robust, observable, and leak-free concurrency model. This is how modern, high-scale Java services are built today.
